title: Tack-weld a T-joint square: hold a steel coupon on edge and TIG-tack it at three marks
instruction: Tack the loose coupon to the base plate as a T-joint on the scribed line, square, with a TIG tack at each of the three marks. Leave it standing on its tacks with the torch back on its rest and your hands clear.
context: Most people have seen welding, in a school shop, on a building site or in welding videos online: a blue-white arc behind a dark lens and a bright bead left behind. This is the step before the weld, and anyone who has tried it knows why it is hard. The welder first tacks the parts with a few short welds that hold them in place. On a T-joint that takes two hands doing different things at once: one holds a loose steel plate on edge, square and on its line, by feel, while the other brings the arc into the corner about 3 mm from the metal without the tungsten touching either plate. Let go too early and the first tack's shrinkage pulls the plate over; hold it crooked and the tack freezes it crooked. Viewers can judge the result at a glance (a plate standing square on three small tacks, both hands clear) and can see what makes it hard: steadiness, two hands in step, inches from an arc.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x away from the arms) and the table's centre line (y toward the left arm); heights are above the table. A steel fixture-table top (29 x 27 cm, 12 mm thick, dark grey, a 50 mm hole grid; x 11.5 to 40.5, y -13.5 to 13.5) lies on the station table. On it a mild-steel base plate (150 x 100 x 6.35 mm; x 19.5 to 34.5, y -11 to -1; top 18.35 mm up) is held by two blue steel strap clamps at its ends (bars 20 x 8 mm reaching 18 mm over the plate at y -9). A joint line is scribed on it along x at y -5.68, from x 23.19 to 30.81 with a cross tick at each end, and three white paint ticks (3 x 16 mm) lie 1 cm left of the line at x 24.79, 27.0 and 29.21: the tack marks, 16 mm from each end and the middle. The coupon is 76.2 x 76.2 x 6.35 mm (3 x 3 x 1/4 in) mild steel, 0.289 kg, saw-cut from hot-rolled flat bar: two saw-cut ends and two rolled edges rounded 1.5 mm, so the flat it stands on is 3.35 mm wide. It lies flat, centred at (25.0, -21.5), on a steel block (40 x 70 x 30 mm) that it overhangs by 18 mm at each saw-cut end, rolled edges toward and away from the base plate. The TIG torch (255 g) lies on two steel posts (45 mm tall) on a steel base, its glass-filled nylon grip block (30 x 36 x 26 mm, orange) centred at (20, 21): a 22 mm rubber-covered handle 11 cm long with a 4 cm stub of cable behind, a black head 24 mm across with its axis 17.5 degrees from vertical, a pink ceramic cup (14 to 18 mm across, 25 mm long) and a 2.4 mm tungsten sticking out 8 mm, pointing along +x, the way the joint runs. Steel on steel friction 0.5. Both grippers start open at the ready pose. The screenshot shows the start. Real trial, fixed settings (full list, costs, checks and safety in the README): a DC TIG inverter, electrode negative, high-frequency start, 130 A, no filler (fusion tacks); 2.4 mm 2% lanthanated tungsten at 8 mm stick-out through a gas lens; argon at 10 L/min; the torch lead on an overhead balancer; coupon and base plate ground bright 15 mm each side of the joint and degreased; the fixture table on insulating pads with the work clamp on it; insulating heat-resistant pads on the holding fingers. The supervisor, outside the welding curtains, holds a hold-to-run arc switch, closing it only while the tungsten is within 10 mm of the joint's root at a mark; one emergency stop cuts the robots' power and the inverter's output. Nobody is inside the curtains; shade 5-8 filters cover the camera lenses; a fume arm draws from beside the joint.
scoring: Read at the end of the run; nothing ends it early. Real trial: read once the parts are under 50 C, nothing moved (how each reading is made: README). A tack is sound at a mark when weld metal fused to both plates across the root lies within 6 mm of the mark along the line (steel ruler) and within 10 mm of the line, with no crack under a 10x loupe, and it is not overheated: no longer than 12 mm and no undercut deeper than 0.5 mm. Faults: tungsten contamination (grey metal on its point, or the point blunted, under the loupe); an overheated tack; stray fused metal or an arc strike more than 10 mm from every mark. Fit, measured on the finished joint: within 2 degrees of square (a machinist's square on the base plate against the coupon's left face at each end: a 2.4 mm feeler must not enter between blade and coupon 70 mm up, or at the foot); root gap 1 mm or less (a 1.0 mm feeler enters nowhere under the coupon's edge); the coupon's left face within 1.5 mm of the scribed line at both ends and its ends within 3 mm of the end ticks (steel ruler). 0 if the coupon or the torch is off the table; 0 with no sound tack; 0 if the coupon is not a T on the joint: more than 10 degrees from square (12 mm at 70 mm up), more than 10 mm off the line, or no edge on the base plate. 0.15 per sound tack (0.15, 0.30, 0.45) when the fit is out of tolerance or a gripper is within 6 cm of the coupon (still held). 0.2 + 0.2 per sound tack (0.4, 0.6, 0.8) when the coupon stands still by its tacks, both grippers 6 cm or more from it, and the fit is in tolerance. Any fault caps the score at 0.4. 1.0 with three sound tacks, the fit in tolerance, no fault, the torch back on its rest (grip centre within 12 mm in plan and 6 mm in height of its rest position, tilted under 10 degrees, turned under 20 degrees), both grippers 6 cm or more from the coupon and the torch, and coupon and torch still for the last 1 s. Simulation stand-ins (full criteria in the README): a root is wherever a coupon edge lies on the base plate with a gap of 1 mm or less; the arc is on while the torch is in a hand (fingertip midpoint within 2.5 cm of its grip centre) and the tungsten tip is 1.5 to 4.5 mm from the nearest root point; each 2 mm of root within 4 mm of that point gains the arc time, is fused at 1.5 s and overheated at 5 s. When metal fuses, the coupon is joined to the bench at that point in the pose it has then: a pin with a bending spring of 0.5 N m per degree that cracks at 2 degrees (1.0 N m); a cracked tack lets go and does not count. Shrinkage is a criterion: if a tack sets while no gripper holds the coupon (both fingers of one gripper, not the torch's, pressing on it with 0.5 N or more each, from the simulator's contact forces; a hand near it or closed round it without touching does not count) and no earlier tack holds it, the joint is set 3 degrees toward the tack's side and pulls the coupon there. Contamination: the tip within 0.5 mm of the base plate, the fixture table or the coupon; latched, and no arc after it.
reset_notes: Simulation: the coupon back flat on its block, the torch on its posts; tacks are cleared at reset. Real trial, consumed each time: a new coupon and a new base plate (or the old one with the tacks ground flush and the line, ticks and marks re-scribed and re-painted), both ground bright and degreased; check the tungsten with the loupe and regrind it after any contamination, keeping 8 mm of stick-out. Handle the parts with tongs until they read under 50 C. Consumables cost about $2 to $6 a trial (README).
fidelity: Rigid bodies with real contact for coupon, base plate, torch and hands. Arc and heat are not simulated: the arc is a tip-to-root distance window with the torch held; a tack is 1.5 s of it where the root gap is 1 mm or less, and becomes a real joint (pin plus 0.5 N m/deg bending spring, cracking at 2 degrees). Weld shrinkage is a criterion, not thermal simulation: a first tack on a coupon no gripper presses on (contact forces) sets 3 degrees toward its side. No glare, gas, cable drag or filler.
scores: Scripted demo: 1.0 (833 steps). Dream-1: 0.0 at the 1,800-step limit (the arms never picked up the torch or the coupon).
